36 [uncertain: Concept] of a letter to the wife of Mr Councillor of War von Triebenfeld, née Reichts[?] — nothing has pained me so much for a long time as Your otherwise esteemed letter of the [illegible] of last month, which I received yesterday; since, namely, I was obliged to gather from it that it would be impossible for the same to cast a suspicion upon the manner of acting I have observed towards you, which yet cannot be other than good and suited to our friendly relations, and has never at any time been otherwise. May this sincere expression of my feeling serve Your [etc.] as a convincing proof — if any such were still needed towards you — how firmly founded my high regard and friendship towards you are, and how much I wish that the same might view from the single correct side that which I shall have the honour to convey to you in what follows.

I perceive with much distress from Your [etc.] letter that the same do not at all regard the measures I took concerning the [illegible] of your Rthl

in the way I wished and intended for your reassurance; on which account I find it necessary to set the particulars out for you most plainly.

It was, namely, in January 1807 that the [uncertain: Justes] Eysach arrived here from Berlin, and [came] to arrange with me a debt proceeding from earlier times. Greatly as this incommoded me, I nevertheless had grounds which determined me to apply every possible means to satisfy this man as to his demand. This was done through the mediation of the privy councillor Major, who is an old acquaintance of Eysenhardt, and with sacrifices on my part which pained me beyond measure.

This took place several weeks later than I had received from You the well-known order to pay for 6,000 Rthl [uncertain: from Szczecin], and since Eysenhardt entered into the arrangement noted above under

no other condition than that I pay him, who stood urgently in need of the money, the [uncertain: Kienier] of 2,500 Rthl in cash against his demand; I therefore seized upon the expedient of making over to him, by cession from me and by endorsement from the privy councillor Mayer, the instrument held by You, under the condition that he should hand over to me in cash the remainder of 3,500 Rthl after collection of the whole 6,000 Rthl. This I did the less scrupulously in that, as You can easily convince yourself, I could at that time not know the very least of the stoppage of payment brought about by the same. I therefore [expected] quite calmly to receive my money from Mr Eysenhardt, when from the same I first received the most highly

unexpected news, [that] the payments to be made had been stopped.

My embarrassment was thereby — I confess it to You — great in more than one respect, inasmuch as I partly stood most urgently in need of the expected 3,500 Rthl, but partly also had to foresee that sooner or later I should have to pay the 2,500 Rthl due to Eysenhardt in some other way. Nevertheless I also took the requisite steps in Wrocław, in accordance with Your wish, likewise to stop the payment of the

6,000 Rthl. This is the true course of this affair up to the present point of time, and I have, and [illegible] to justify myself most fully to You, now only to add what I have further done in this matter with regard to Your wishes.

When, namely, I received your letter of the [blank], in which the same wished the [uncertain: return] of the oft-mentioned instrument, I at once resolved — since I have no more eager [desire] than to show You in all things how much I [strive] to comply with your wishes —

to procure the same for him again forthwith, be it at the greatest sacrifice. And since I still had about as much to draw, from the moneys that had been deposited for the [uncertain: war office], as the sum assigned to Mr Eysenhardt amounted to, I accordingly, upon receipt of the letter from [blank], requested Assessor Koppe in writing, [illegible] [illegible], to pay Mr Eysenhardt without delay the sum owing to him, the 2,500 Rthl, out of the above money, and in return to take back the instrument from [uncertain: him] (which Mr Major-General Amelang has in safekeeping), and to deliver the same to You. Since Assessor Koppe is now back, as letters from Heidelberg, where he passed through, inform me, I therefore regard my commission to him as executed and Your wish in this matter as fulfilled. You will be pleased to convince yourself from the exact narrative of events given above that I have done absolutely nothing in this affair that does not bear the stamp of the greatest high regard and friendship towards the same,

and that therefore the expressions contained, as the same say, in the [uncertain: Mayndl.] letter do not proceed from me, nor was it in any way my intention to wish to present the matter from the side in which You have taken it up, since I shall rather always be most highly grateful to you for that which the same have done for me (as out of friendship).

This assurance, then, You will not be able to refuse the fullest belief, when I have the honour [uncertain: to report] to you herewith, that I am sending you

the amount of 3,000 Rthl Courant demanded in Your last letter of the 25th of last month. You etc. may believe that I thereby deprive myself of almost my last moneys, in order to comply with Your wishes, and truly nothing less than the strength of my attachment to you was needed to resolve upon this step also. I now beg the same to bring the whole affair entirely to effect, and to send me the earliest news of it.

The enclosed Rthl to Amelang you will be pleased to have forwarded to the authority, although I may at the same time expect that the return of the instrument will already have taken place.

From Your honoured letter I might almost suppose that the same do not stand on the best terms with the minister [uncertain: Er.] von Stein; I must sincerely confess to the same that this would pain me greatly, since I believe that this gentleman is one of those who must in every case be spared.

I should much wish that you might give me the pleasure, on your journey to Vienna, of visiting me here yourself; this would be quite extraordinarily welcome to me, inasmuch as it is not possible to settle in writing everything upon which I should very gladly hear your advice and upon which I should like to have information from you. Gladly would I have resolved for this purpose to send a confidential person to you, but I was solely

held back by the thought that You might perhaps not gladly say to anyone other than myself all that would be worth my knowing. I know therefore of no other means than an express visit from You here, which would not occasion too great a detour, since you are in any case travelling by way of Dresden, and I therefore most urgently request the same, wherever it be at all possible,

to give me this pleasure. Should you find it advisable to say something of it to Mr Assessor Koppe, I beg you to do so. In respect of the money business I am not idle here, only I cannot say anything further about it before the lapse of 8–14 days, because various papers are still wanting for it, which I expect daily. I beg you only to see to it that the cession of the mortgage may take place at once, if such be required, so that the business meet with no [obstacle] on that account. I have ordered my [uncertain: court agent] here to report [illegible] in [illegible], on which account I the more wish that the same might await his arrival at Berlin, since I believe he would be [illegible] of use in a money business very much to be wished for by me.

What I received yesterday in respect of the [uncertain: Wildegan], I send You herewith in copy, with the request that you instruct me what is perhaps to be done in the matter, and also, in order to give the occasion, that You might herein set in train the [uncertain: step] appearing serviceable to you.

With the same request you receive herewith [the proposal] which was made as a proposal [illegible] of a [uncertain: contract] by [uncertain: Jeg.], and I very much request the same to let me have your opinion and advice upon it at the earliest.

Your Right Honourable

Öhringen, 13 March 1808. To Your Right Honourable Mr Councillor of War von Triebenfeld.

summary_en: Letter to von Triebenfeld, partly illegible. The writer defends his handling of the order for 6,000 Rthl: he says Eysenhardt demanded 2,500 Rthl in cash in January 1807 on account of an old debt and received the order in return for repayment of 3,500 Rthl. After payment was suspended, the writer says he instructed Assessor Koppe to pay Eysenhardt and to take back the order held in safekeeping by Amelang. He sends the 3,000 Rthl Courant demanded and asks for a visit on the journey to Vienna.
summary_de: Schreiben an v. Triebenfeld, teils unleserlich. Der Schreiber rechtfertigt sein Vorgehen mit der Anweisung über 6000 Rthl: Eysenhardt verlangte im Januar 1807 wegen einer alten Schuld 2500 Rthl bar und erhielt dafür die Anweisung gegen Rückzahlung von 3,500 Rthl. Nach der Zahlungssistierung beauftragte der Schreiber Assessor Koppe, Eysenhardt zu bezahlen und die bei Amelang verwahrte Anweisung zurückzunehmen. Er schickt die geforderten 3000 Rthl Courant und bittet um einen Besuch auf der Reise nach Wien.

reading.notes: A copy of a letter to Krieges Rath v. Triebenfeld, written at Öhringen. The writer is not named. He answers a hurt letter from Triebenfeld and explains what he did with a 6000 Rthl Anweisung. In January 1807 Eysenhardt came from Berlin about an old debt and wanted 2500 Rthl in cash. The writer ceded the Anweisung to him on condition that he pay back 3500 Rthl once he had collected it. Then payment was stopped (sistirt). The writer has told Assessor Koppe to pay Eysenhardt the 2500 Rthl and take the Anweisung back from Amelang. He sends the 3000 Rthl Courant that was asked for, voices concern about relations with Minister v. Stein, and invites Triebenfeld to visit on his way to Wien via Dresden. Heavily garbled. Nothing on Trąbczyn.
